doc.title: Joe Wilder Part 2 interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 12, 1998

title: Musicians and business people today: Fillius and the Maxine Sullivan date
summary: Some promoters like Milt Fillius treat musicians with respect, but Wilder hung up on a caller offering sideman scale for Maxine Sullivan's last recording.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: How is the actual business — it seems that there are too many stories about business people taking advantage of musicians over the years. Have you experienced that and has it changed?

Well I think it’s changed and for instance, as in the case of the jazz party you have here at Hamilton, especially with people like Milt Fillius. I mean these are men who are proud of who they are and they want people who work for them to feel proud of having been associated with him. I’m using him as an example. There are a few others, there aren’t many, but there are some others who think likewise. And they treat the musicians very well, with a great deal of respect, and of course they expect the same in return. But they’re the exceptions. There are a lot of people who still think, for instance I was called to do a recording with Maxine Sullivan which turned out to be her last recording, and I would gladly have done it for nothing basically. But the fellow who called me, when he called me and said that she had asked if I could do a recording with her, and I said I’d be flattered to do it. I said, “by the way, how much are you paying?” And he said, “hey, Joe, we pay sideman scale.” And I won’t mention his name. I said, “well you’ve got it.” Boom and I just hung up on him. Now these are guys who still think it’s the 20’s and the 30’s and musicians are struggling as they did during that period and would accept almost anything, whatever you offered you know, and you dictate the terms not they you know.
